3. The government as defendant No.1 contested the said suit by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that the suit land is government Khas land and is part of the Bazar namely Zamindar Hat. The said land has been recorded in Khas Khatian No.1 during SA and MRR operation, All the Bazars became khas land and were vested to the government from 1st Baishak 1368 BS as per The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the government has been leasing out the said Bazar since 1368 BS Accordingly during preparation of MRR Kkatian the same has been recorded as Hat in the name of the Government, The plaintiff never possessed the suit land and, as such, he has no right, title or interest over the suit land, hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. The suit land is being possessed by the defendant No. 7, who constructed a grocery shop thereon and subsequently applied for lease of the Suit land. 

 12. Again, on plain reading of DS Khatian No.58 (Exhibit 3) it appears that the suit plot No.2141 was recorded in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff's father named Swarup Chandra Bhuiyan from whom the plaintiff's father purchased the suit land in benami of the defendant No.7. It also appears from the Exhibit-3 that the nature of the suit land had been described in DS Khatian as orchard'. Had the suit land been part of Hat then it should have been written to the same effect. The plaintiff claimed that he used to cut down the trees on the suit land from time to time and for the said reason the suit land was vacant land. PW 2 also stated in his deposition that the suit land was orchard. In the similar way, PW 3 deposed supporting the deposition of PWs 1 and 2 regarding the said assertion. It was argued on behalf of the defendant No.1 that the suit land being in close proximity to a Bazaar and said Bazaar had later on extended to the suit land. But the said claim of the defendant No.1 was not supported by the evidence on record. On the other hand, it is settled principle of law that mere recording of the suit land in the name of the defendant No.1 without proof of title does not devolve any ownership of the suit land upon the defendant No. l. In the light of the discussion made above, it is crystal clear that the plaintiff has title and possession of the suit land prior to dispossession on 18-11-1980. 

 14. In view of the foregoing discussion, the trial Court on proper appraisal of the oral evidence as well as documentary evidence available on the record decreed the suit. The appellate Court and the High Court Division also most legally upheld the judgment and decree of the trial Court. We do not find any perversion in the impugned judgment and decree and, as such, we are impelled to hold that the plaintiff has acquired a valid title and possession in the suit land and during the pendency of suit the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendants No.8-10. Due to reasons stated above, it does not warrant interference with the judgment and decree dated 10-5-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3151 of 1998. Therefore, we do not find any merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant and, as such, the instant Civil Appeal is liable to be dismissed.
